newsitem.title: USA: Gold demand at historic high - US Gold Institute.
newsitem.headline: Gold demand at historic high - US Gold Institute.

text.p: Worldwide demand for gold is at an historic high and is about 44 percent above total annual production of the world's gold mines, the US Gold Institute said Monday.
"While this is good news for all gold-producing countries, it is especially good news for the U.S.," Gold Institute president John Lutley said.
"Because of higher productivity and competitiveness, the U.S. is poised to capture the largest share of the expanding world market," he said.
"By 1998 the U.S. will be almost even with South Africa, the worlds largest gold producer, in total production at approximately 14 million ounces."
Lutley was commenting on the release of the Institute's biennial report on the U.S. gold industry, prepared by John Dobra of the Natural Resource Industry Institute, at the University of Nevada.
The report forecast a 20 percent increase in U.S. gold production over the next two years.
A resurgence in capital spending on exploration and development is expected to bring about 43 million ounces of new reserves into production by 1999, the report said.
But the development of new underground mines, with higher ore grades, will reduce production costs per ounce, compared with the current open-pit mines, the report said.
The study said that U.S. production in 1995, though down slightly from the three previous years, exceeded 10 million ounces for the fourth consecutive year.
Average return on equity for U.S. gold miners rose slightly to 5.47 percent from 5.25 percent.
About two-thirds of total U.S. output comes from the state of Nevada, with the balance from California, Utah, South Dakota, Montana, Alaska and South Carolina.
Almost 40 percent of U.S. gold output in 1995, or 3.9 million ounces, came from the operations on the Carlin Trend in north-central Nevada owned by Barrick Gold Corp and Newmont Gold Co, Dobra said.
The total value of U.S. gold output in 1995 was $3.91 billion.
During 1996 and 1996 gold production provided over 110,900 jobs, an increase of 25 percent on 1994, the report said.

Nearly 21,000 jobs were provided in states across the country that provide equipment and services to the gold mining industry, including 6,000 jobs in Illinois alone, where two major heavy equipment manufacturers are based.
"The gold mining industry contributes more than half a billion dollars in federal and state income taxes every year," Lutley said.
